details:
**Mrs. Dalloway**
Woolf's 1925 stream-of-consciousness novel set over a single June day in London after World War I. The society hostess Clarissa Dalloway goes to buy flowers on Bond Street and prepares for the party she gives that evening, where she learns of the suicide of a young man she never met. Clarissa has a "perpetual sense" of being "out, out, far out to sea and alone," and was first explored in the short story "Mrs. Dalloway in Bond Street."

**Septimus Warren Smith**
The shell-shocked World War I veteran who is Clarissa's double in Mrs. Dalloway. He hallucinates his dead friend and officer Evans in Regent's Park and kills himself by jumping out of the window of his lodgings as the doctor Holmes comes to take him away. Clarissa hears of his death at her party and reflects on it.

**Sally Seton and Peter Walsh**
Figures from Clarissa's youth at Bourton. Clarissa remembers kissing the bold Sally Seton as "the most exquisite moment of her whole life." Peter Walsh, whom she refused to marry in favor of Richard Dalloway, returns from India and visits her on the day of the party. Other details: Clarissa's daughter Elizabeth is drawn to the religious tutor Doris Kilman, whom Clarissa dislikes, and early in the novel a car backfires on Bond Street while an airplane skywrites letters that people read as "toffee." Michael Cunningham's novel The Hours (1998) reworks Mrs. Dalloway and features Woolf herself.

**To the Lighthouse**
Woolf's 1927 novel set at the Ramsay family's summer house on the Isle of Skye in Scotland. In the first section, "The Window," young James Ramsay wants to sail to the lighthouse, but his father, the philosopher Mr. Ramsay, insists the weather will not allow it. In the final section, "The Lighthouse," years later, Mr. Ramsay finally sails there with James and Cam, who have resolved not to speak to him.

**Lily Briscoe and Charles Tansley**
Lily Briscoe is the unmarried painter staying with the Ramsays who tries to paint Mrs. Ramsay, representing her as a purple triangle, and finally completes the painting at the end of the novel. The awkward young philosopher Charles Tansley, a guest of Mr. Ramsay, keeps repeating "Women can't paint, women can't write," which haunts Lily.

**"Time Passes"**
The short middle section of To the Lighthouse, covering about ten years during which the empty house decays. Major events appear only in square brackets: Mrs. Ramsay dies suddenly, her daughter Prue dies from complications of childbirth, and her son Andrew is killed by a shell in World War I.

**A Room of One's Own**
Woolf's 1929 feminist essay, based on lectures she gave at Cambridge women's colleges, arguing that "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction," specifically five hundred pounds a year. It imagines Judith Shakespeare, William's equally gifted sister, whose talent is crushed by society and who kills herself.

**"Chloe liked Olivia" and other scenes from A Room of One's Own**
The narrator praises the sentence "Chloe liked Olivia" from an imagined novel by Mary Carmichael, because it shows a relationship between two women. At the fictional "Oxbridge," a beadle orders her off the grass and back onto the gravel path, sending the "little fish" of her thought into hiding, and she is turned away from the library because she is a woman; she also laughs while wondering whether men hummed Tennyson at luncheon parties before the war.

**Orlando**
Woolf's 1928 mock-biography of a young Elizabethan nobleman who lives for over 300 years, until 1928, and wakes up a woman while serving as ambassador to Constantinople. Orlando lives with a band of Romani, almost causes a sailor to fall from the rigging by showing her ankle (and cries "Praise God that I'm a woman!"), skates on the frozen Thames during the Great Frost, and works for centuries on the poem "The Oak Tree."

**Vita Sackville-West and the Hogarth Press**
Woolf's lover, the writer Vita Sackville-West, inspired Orlando. Woolf and her husband Leonard Woolf founded the Hogarth Press, which published Woolf's own books and had commercial success with Sackville-West's novels such as Seducers in Ecuador and The Edwardians. Woolf was a central figure of the Bloomsbury Group.

**The Waves**
Woolf's 1931 experimental novel, which she called a "playpoem," made up of soliloquies by six friends, including Bernard, Neville, and Rhoda, interspersed with italic descriptions of the sun moving over the sea. The seventh friend, Percival, never speaks; his death in India from a fall from his horse is related by the others, and Bernard compares the friends to a six-sided flower.

**Flush**
Woolf's 1933 mock-biography of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's cocker spaniel, Flush. The jealous dog bites Elizabeth's suitor Robert Browning at her home on Wimpole Street before accompanying the couple to Italy.

**Jacob's Room**
Woolf's 1922 novel, the first of her experimental novels, published by the Hogarth Press. It portrays the young man Jacob Flanders only through the impressions of others, such as the women Clara Durrant and Florinda, and ends after his death in World War I with his mother holding up his empty shoes.

**"The Death of the Moth," "How Should One Read a Book?", and Freshwater**
In the essay "The Death of the Moth," Woolf watches a moth's struggle against death at a windowpane. In "How Should One Read a Book?" she advises readers to give the writer "the benefit of every doubt" at first, and later to "judge with the utmost severity." Her comic play Freshwater satirizes her great-aunt, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, and the Tennyson circle on the Isle of Wight.

**Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?**
Edward Albee's 1962 play, whose title puns on Woolf's name and the song "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?" The history professor George and his wife Martha torment their young guests, the biology professor Nick and his wife Honey, through a night of drinking, and George finally "kills" the couple's imaginary son.
